title: The plant reproduction strategy studio
subtitle: Compare gamete fusion with runners and cuttings
objective: Distinguish sexual and asexual plant reproduction using process evidence rather than the number of visible parent plants.

sow.exactOutcome: Describe sexual and asexual reproduction in plants.
sow.alignment: New outcome; sexual reproduction is gamete fusion, not necessarily two separate parent plants. Original secondary-age exemplar at an upper-KS2 conceptual level; no qualification approval or completion claim.

priorLearning: Know that offspring inherit genetic information.
success: Identify whether gamete fusion occurs in a case.
Describe a runner or cutting as an asexual route.
Explain why sexual reproduction can involve one self-pollinating plant.

vocabulary.meaning: A horizontal stem that can produce a new plant at a node.
A piece of a parent plant used to grow a new plant.
An offspring with the same inherited genetic information as its source, apart from changes such as mutations.
Differences among individuals; genes and environment can contribute.

equipment: Plant case cards, selected route, pencils; optional paper runner model.
preparation: Use the case’s stated reproductive process, not just appearance or number of plants.
No live cutting or rooting chemical is needed.
safety: Use paper models; no plant tasting, cutting tools or hormone powder.
practicalAlternative: All decisions use supplied cases and diagrams. A live propagation experiment is not required or claimed completed.

misconceptions.claim: Sexual reproduction always needs two separate parent plants.
misconceptions.correction: Some flowers can self-pollinate and self-fertilise; gamete fusion is still sexual reproduction.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether gametes fuse in the case.

misconceptions.claim: Every seed must be sexual and every clone looks identical.
misconceptions.correction: Some plants form asexual seeds; environment can alter the appearance of genetically similar plants.
misconceptions.check: Ask what process is actually stated.

misconceptions.claim: Asexual offspring can never vary at all.
misconceptions.correction: They are usually genetically very similar clones, but mutations and environmental effects can produce differences.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether different growth conditions could change height.

access.supported: Sort stated gamete-fusion cases and explain one runner.
access.standard: Compare processes and choose a nursery plan using evidence.
access.stretch: Evaluate self-fertilisation, clone and all-seeds claims.
access.regulation: Offer private writing, pointing, drawing or adult scribing. Allow pass-and-return for public questions and desk-based participation. Choose support from current learning evidence, not fixed ability labels.

sources.title: OpenStax Biology 2e: Pollination and fertilization
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Pollination differs from gamete fusion; fertilised ovule develops into seed and ovary into fruit. College detail is selectively simplified for GROW.

sources.title: OpenStax Biology 2e: Asexual reproduction
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Runners, cuttings and clonal reproduction. Some plants can produce asexual seeds; core examples identify the actual process.

sources.title: RHS: How plants reproduce
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Sexual and clonal propagation overview; plants may use more than one reproductive strategy.

slides.title: One visible parent: one answer?
body: A new plant grows near one parent.
Can you identify the reproduction type from that alone?
slides.notes: No: need process evidence. The lesson’s central question is whether gametes fuse, not merely counting visible plants.

slides.title: Recover the fusion event
body: R1. What is fertilisation?
R2. What develops into a seed after fertilisation?
R3. Is growth of one plant the same as producing offspring?
slides.notes: Gamete fusion; fertilised ovule; no. Do not treat every natural seed as necessarily sexual.

slides.title: I look for gamete fusion
body: Fusion identifies sexual reproduction.
Gametes can come from one self-fertile plant.
Two separate plants are not the defining rule.
slides.notes: Think aloud with case B: I see only one parent plant, but the record says gametes fuse. Therefore it is sexual reproduction. A self-fertile plant can supply both gametes.

visual.title: Sexual reproduction: the defining event
visual.description:
A simplified scientific sequence: Male gamete; Fusion with
female gamete; Offspring
with inherited
genes. Gametes may come from different plants
or from one self-fertile plant.

elements.text:
Gametes may come from different plants
or from one self-fertile plant.

slides.title: I trace the runner route
body: The new plant grows from a parent stem.
No gametes fuse in this runner route.
This is asexual reproduction.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Trace runner from parent to rooted node. The runner is a stem, not a root stretching between unrelated plants. It can remain attached during early growth.

visual.title: Strawberry runner: new plant from a stem
visual.description: An original strawberry plant is connected by a horizontal runner to a rooted daughter plant. Both are shown above the same ground line; no gamete fusion is required in this vegetative route.

elements.text: A runner can produce a daughter plant
Vegetative growth from the parent; no gamete fusion here.

slides.title: I separate genetic similarity from appearance
body: A cutting can produce a clone of its source.
Conditions can affect size and appearance.
“Clone” does not mean every visible feature is fixed.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Use illustrative growth model, not measured trial data. Explain that mutation is a possible genetic change; supported pupils need only avoid the never-varies claim.

visual.title: Genes and environment are different influences
visual.description: Two rooted cuttings from the same parent are drawn with different heights under different growth conditions. The comparison illustrates that clonal genetic similarity does not guarantee identical appearance.

elements.text: Illustrative model: genes and growth conditions both affect traits.

slides.title: Nursery case conference
body: W1. Sort A–D using gamete fusion.
Give the evidence phrase that decides each case.
Do not count parent plants alone.
slides.notes: A/B sexual; C/D asexual. Pupils move labels or vote privately, then justify using the case wording.

slides.title: Choose a plan for the nursery
body: W2. The nursery wants inherited mint features retained.
Recommend the stated cutting route or a new cross.
Give one reason and one condition to control.
slides.notes: Cuttings preserve the source’s inherited features more directly; seed crosses can introduce genetic variation. Keep suitable light/water/temperature consistent; clones do not guarantee identical growth or immunity.

slides.title: Challenge the shortcut rules
body: W3. Repair “one parent always means asexual”.
Then repair “all clones always look identical”.
slides.notes: Case B contradicts the first; environment/mutation limits second. Accept concise bounded explanations.
slides.reveal: Use the fusion evidence. A self-fertile plant can reproduce sexually; clone appearance can vary.

slides.title: A flower self-fertilises
body: Its male and female gametes fuse. Which route is this?
slides.notes: Sexual reproduction occurs because gametes fuse; it is not defined by the number of separate plants and is more than ordinary growth.

options.feedback: Gamete fusion is the defining event, even with one parent plant.

options.text: Asexual because only one parent plant is visible.
options.feedback: Counting plants misses the fusion event.
A new offspring develops after fertilisation.

slides.title: Your independent investigation
body: Choose one route.
Use the stated process to classify each case.
Explain a nursery decision and its limits.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across the three You do slides. Supply shared page 1 and one selected route page. All routes target the stated science objective; a labelled drawing or independent dictated explanation is valid.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Underline “gametes fuse” or “no fusion”.
Name runner or cutting when relevant.
Separate genes from growth conditions.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Ask pupils which evidence supports their explanation. Read prompts or scribe without supplying the scientific conclusion.

slides.title: Check before sharing
body: Does my explanation answer the question?
Have I named the evidence or process?
Have I kept the conclusion within its limits?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Use the route-specific worked answers to identify one precise next step.

slides.title: Compare and improve
body: Share one classification and reason.
Check a broad rule against the case cards.
Improve an absolute clone claim.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Offer partner or private teacher feedback. Ask for one specific revision linked to evidence; no public ranking.

slides.title: A question worth investigating
body: Suggest one next question about this lesson’s evidence.
Choose a question whose answer would improve our model.
slides.notes: Lundy cycle: invite written, spoken or pointed suggestions. Select one feasible question and explain how the pupil contribution changes the next example or investigation.

slides.title: Show the science you can explain
body: E1. What distinguishes sexual reproduction?
E2. Give one asexual plant method.
E3. Can self-fertilisation be sexual? Explain.
slides.notes: Fusion; runner/cutting; yes, gametes fuse. E4 asks why clones may look different.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: nursery cases
pupilPages.intro: Cases are constructed teaching examples using the stated biological processes.

cards.title: A • Crossed flowers
cards.text: Pollen from one pea plant reaches another. A male and female gamete fuse before the seed develops.

cards.title: B • Self-fertile flower
cards.text: A flower receives its own plant’s pollen. Male and female gametes fuse before a seed develops.

cards.title: C • Strawberry runner
cards.text: A horizontal stem grows from a parent. It roots at a node and forms a daughter plant without gamete fusion.

cards.title: D • Mint cutting
cards.text: A piece of a parent stem roots and grows into a new plant. No gamete fusion occurs in this route.

cards.title: E • Nursery brief
cards.text: A fictional nursery wants to preserve a parent mint plant’s inherited features. It can use cuttings; growth conditions still need care.

cards.title: F • Limits card
cards.text: Clones usually share inherited information, apart from changes such as mutations. Conditions affect appearance. Some plants can make seeds without fertilisation; identify the stated process.

blocks.prompt: W1. Sort A–D into sexual/asexual and cite the deciding phrase.
W2. Recommend a route for the mint nursery and one condition to control.
W3. Repair the one-parent and identical-clone rules.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: find the fusion
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Word bank: sexual / asexual / gametes / runner.

blocks.prompt: S1. In case B, gametes fuse. Is this sexual or asexual?
S2. A strawberry runner grows a daughter plant without fusion. Is this sexual or asexual?
S3. Complete: Sexual reproduction involves ____ fusing. A ____ can form a new plant without that fusion.
S4. Which method could retain the mint parent’s inherited features: cutting or a new cross? Explain.
S5. Give one reason two clones might look different.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: nursery decision
pupilPages.intro: Use the process evidence, not a visual parent count.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the case table.
N2. Explain why case B is sexual despite one parent plant.
N3. Recommend a method for the mint brief. Give a reason and one growth condition to control.
N4. Repair “clones always look identical”.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: test the definitions
pupilPages.intro: Avoid all/never claims unsupported by the stated cases.

blocks.prompt: T1. Compare sexual and asexual reproduction using fusion, inherited information and one named method.
T2. Explain why “two parents versus one” is an unreliable complete definition for plants.
T3. A plant forms seeds without gamete fusion. Which reproduction category fits the stated evidence? Explain.
T4. Evaluate a nursery promise: “Every cutting will look identical and resist every disease.” Give a better claim and one practical limitation.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Short reasons matter more than labels alone.

blocks.prompt: E1. What event defines sexual reproduction?
E2. Describe one asexual plant method.
E3. Can one self-fertile plant reproduce sexually? Explain.
E4. Why might genetically similar clones look different?
Reflection. Which nursery question needs more evidence?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: Gamete fusion; fertilised ovule; growth develops one individual while reproduction produces offspring.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: A/B sexual because gametes fuse; C/D asexual because no fusion. W2 cutting for retaining source genetic features, with controlled suitable growth conditions. W3 self-fertilisation is a one-parent sexual case; clones can differ through environment and sometimes mutation.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A correct; B incorrectly counts visible parents; C ignores production of offspring.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 sexual. S2 asexual. S3 gametes; runner. S4 cutting, because it develops vegetatively from the source and usually retains its genetic information. S5 different environment or mutation; an accurate example such as different light is sufficient.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: A sexual/fusion; B sexual/fusion; C asexual/no fusion via runner; D asexual/no fusion via cutting. N2 gamete fusion defines the route. N3 cutting plus retained inherited features and relevant control. N4 genetically similar plants can respond differently to growth conditions; mutation can also alter inherited information.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 sexual uses fusion and typically produces genetic variation; asexual has no fusion and usually produces clones, e.g. runner/cutting. T2 self-fertilisation can use one plant yet remain sexual. T3 asexual seed formation according to the stated lack of fusion; this prevents treating all seeds as sexual. T4 cuttings usually retain source genes but appearance, establishment and disease outcomes depend on more than that; use suitable conditions and monitor health without guarantees.

answers.label: E1–E4 / assessment
answers.answer: Fusion; accurate runner/cutting description; yes through gamete fusion; conditions or mutation may differ. Secure: correct process definition applied to self-fertilisation and vegetative cases, plus a bounded clone claim. Re-teach classification by highlighting the fusion evidence. Reflection accepts a relevant uncertainty.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.

The defining distinction is gamete fusion. Self-fertilisation remains sexual even if one plant supplies both gametes. Do not teach all seeds as universally sexual; optional asexual seed formation is explicitly signposted.
Paper runner and cutting cards support the same interactive decisions. A propagation practical would require separate ongoing care; this lesson does not claim roots appear within 40 minutes.

interactive.title: Nursery studio: choose from process evidence
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.
